#4563. Latest Update: How Airbnb uses cost per task to operate coding agents on Amazon Bedrock

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2463 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: How Airbnb uses cost per task to operate coding agents on Amazon Bedrock

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2463 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon Bedrock provides access to foundation models from multiple providers through a common API, with AWS managing the model infrastructure.
  • As coding agents move into production, changes in models and usage can affect latency, capacity, and cost.
  • In this post, we show how Airbnb evaluates models for coding agents and monitors their use on Amazon Bedrock.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon Bedrock provides access to foundation models from multiple providers through a common API, with AWS managing the model infrastructure. It integrates with AWS access controls and monitoring, and processes prompts, code, and model responses within AWS.

As coding agents move into production, changes in models and usage can affect latency, capacity, and cost. Amazon Bedrock runtime metrics in Amazon CloudWatch help teams investigate latency increases, throttling, and changes in token consumption. Evaluations, or evals, complement these operational metrics by assessing the quality of an agent’s work on a fixed set of representative tasks.

In this post, we show how Airbnb evaluates models for coding agents and monitors their use on Amazon Bedrock. We explain how cost per task guides model selection and how production data helps us revisit those choices as usage changes. We also describe the runtime signals used to investigate latency, throttling, and spend.

At Airbnb, thousands of engineers and engineering-adjacent people use AirChat, our internal tool for running coding agents, every week. The agents send their model requests through our large language model (LLM) gateway, which runs on Amazon Bedrock. Bedrock processes Airbnb’s code, prompts, and model responses within AWS. Eight new models came out in about five weeks. By mid-October, about two thirds of the requests our engineers sent through coding agents went to those new models.

Each release can change output tokens, cost, latency and capacity at once, and the benchmark charts published with a launch don’t show how a model handles our engineers’ work. So we run two systems side by side. Before a rollout, we run evals on our own tasks to measure each model’s score and cost per task. Cost per task is the list-price cost of all the tokens an agent uses to finish one task.

Industry observers note that after a rollout, observability highlights us what changed in production. When production usage doesn’t match the eval results, we find out why.

You can diagnose most production problems with a few signals in the AWS/Bedrock namespace in CloudWatch:.

Sources indicate that on top of these metrics, we add cost per task. Our evals measure a score and a cost per task for every model and every reasoning effort we allow. Reasoning effort is a setting that controls how much a model reasons before it responds. We use the results to choose each default, which is the model and effort that our coding tools use unless an engineer picks another, and each effort ceiling, which is the highest effort we allow for a model.

Industry observers note that engineers run AirChat on their AirDev workspaces, which are personal development machines in the cloud. They can also hand a task to AirChat Remote, which runs cloud agents in separate cloud workspaces while the engineer does something else. Both paths go through our LLM gateway to Amazon Bedrock.

In a recent development, figure 1 reveals how AirChat and AirChat Remote reach Amazon Bedrock through our gateway. It also shows how evals and production monitoring guide model defaults and effort ceilings.

Figure 1: Coding agents and cloud agents call Amazon Bedrock through our LLM gateway. Our usage records and CloudWatch metrics show real use, and we use eval results to set defaults and effort ceilings.

The gateway records the model, client, team, and user for each request. We use these records only in aggregate, for cost and capacity planning. CloudWatch supplies token counts, latency, errors, and throttles. We compare those production signals with our eval scores and cost per task to decide when defaults or effort ceilings need to change.

Recent findings suggest that tagged IAM roles for your callers, with cost allocation tags activated. Activate them before you start collecting, because activation doesn’t backfill earlier costs.

You also need three things of your own:.

According to recent reports, before rollout, define what the agents can access and which actions need human review. Run code in isolated workspaces and test generated changes before merging. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails can help filter harmful content and sensitive information in prompts and responses. For responses based on supplied reference material, contextual grounding checks can flag unsupported claims. Test these controls on your own tasks and include their latency and cost in your measurements.

Start by measuring what a complete task costs. Then use those results to choose model defaults, check production behavior, manage capacity, and attribute spend.

A coding agent takes many requests to finish one task, and on each request the model re-reads the context so far. So we price the whole task.

In a recent development, bedrock reports four kinds of tokens for each request: uncached input, cache reads, cache writes and output. In an eval run we price all four for every request and add up the requests in the task. Every cost in this post uses the public list prices dated for that run. We record the average cost next to the score for every model, reasoning effort and agent client we test, and the average includes low-scoring attempts.

It has been revealed that reasoning effort changes both score and cost. On one model we tested, moving from low to high effort raised the score by 0.8 points. Cost per task was 2.5 times as high. We use these results to set effort ceilings, which the gateway enforces.

On the afternoon a upcoming model came out, a single request to our agents started an eval campaign, which runs the new model through all our task suites. A suite is a fixed set of tasks of one type, and we have seven. Agents spread hundreds of tasks across the suites and several cloud workspaces, and each result appeared as soon as a grader scored it. First results arrived within hours. By the next morning, every suite had a score and a cost per task, and we had what we needed for a deployment decision for the entire org.

According to recent reports, that speed depends on tasks that are already written down. Each task is a folder that holds everything one run needs. Here is a trimmed task from our machine learning work:.

The grader recomputes the right answer from frozen data on every run, and the agent earns a reward of 1 only if every check passes. To test one model at every effort, list each effort as its own agent in a job config:.

Both examples use the formats of Harbor, an open-source framework for running agent evals in sandboxes. It’s one option if you’re starting out.

Running the evals can be optimized. Writing the rubric, the scoring guide that a grader follows, is the hardest part. Our long tasks run over several rounds, with a simulated reviewer pushing back between rounds. A model grader scores each run on eight weighted dimensions. Each dimension gets a score from 0 to 3.

Because of ceilings like this one, an agent that needed rescuing can’t score well on polish alone.

Recent findings suggest that when latency rises, chart three signals before you open a support case: TimeToFirstToken for the wait before generation starts, OutputTokenCount for response length, and OTPS for generation speed. Bedrock has no native OTPS metric. You derive it with metric math, as the Amazon Bedrock User Guide describes:.

In the example from our session, latency rose 40 percent while time to first token and OTPS stayed flat. Someone had changed the system prompt to ask for more thorough answers, and output tokens per request rose 50 percent. The model generated at the same speed and wrote longer responses. Treat prompt changes and model upgrades as deploys, and mark them on your dashboard.

Each week we put the CloudWatch runtime metrics next to the usage records from our gateway for each model. For cost and capacity planning, we also look at usage in aggregate: cost per request and the average number of requests per user each week. A new model can move both. After every rollout, we compare them with what we expected from the eval’s cost per task.

One model, which we call model A, looked good in our evals. On our coding tasks, it scored more than three points above our previous best model. Cost per task was about the same, and the same grader scored every model. We rolled it out, capped effort at high, and asked people to use low or medium for most work.

A few weeks after launch, we priced model A’s production usage at list price and looked at it in aggregate. Average weekly spend per user was several times higher on model A than on the model before it. Each model A request cost about three times as much, and the average model A user sent about three times as many requests.

Output tokens made up only a tenth of a request’s cost. Most of the cost went to cached context, which the model re-read on every request. Model A could work on its own for a long time, so people started long, self-directed sessions with it.

It has been revealed that the eval measured the model on a task. Production measured how people chose to work with it.

Recent findings suggest that later, a newer model scored higher than model A on the same tasks and grader, at about a sixth of its cost per task. We moved model A’s users to it with a configuration change.

We then checked the change in aggregate on the same user group, the heavy customers of model A. In their first full week on the newer model, the group sent about the same number of requests to their main model, and the group’s spend on that model fell to about a seventh.

According to recent reports, on the bedrock-runtime endpoint, Bedrock checks your tokens-per-minute quota when a request arrives, before the model writes anything. It reserves your uncached input tokens and your cache writes, plus max_tokens, the most output the request is allowed. It adjusts that reservation as the model generates and returns the unused part when the request settles. Cache reads never count against the quota, so a request can be cheap against your quota and expensive on your bill. Output tokens settle at a burndown rate that is 1:1 on most models and several times that on some current models, so check your model’s rate.

A dashboard of billed tokens can show room while requests are being throttled. In our session’s example, the quota was 1 million tokens per minute and traffic was 300 requests per minute. The dashboard indicated about 30 percent of quota. After applying a 5:1 output-token burndown rate, completed requests consumed about 77 percent.

Recent findings suggest that admission uses a different calculation. Each request initially reserved 600 uncached input tokens plus a max_tokens of 4,096, for a total of 4,696 tokens. Responses were about 800 tokens at p99.

Lowering max_tokens to 1,024 cut the initial reservation to 1,624 tokens, about 65 percent smaller. The limit was still above p99. For unchanged input and output, final quota consumption stays the same. The smaller reservation leaves more room to admit requests. Monitor stopReason to catch truncated responses. Use backoff and jitter, and cap retries.

Demand can also outrun the headroom you have on any one model. You want to know where work can go before you need it, and our evals answer that. The answer can be a model from another model family. For every major model we use, we keep at least one equivalent that performs as well on our evals and that we can load-balance to. Without those evals, choosing where the work goes would be guesswork.

In a recent development, if headroom on a model stays tight, we can rebalance by changing a default in our configuration. First check that the equivalent model has capacity for the extra load and that your quota covers it. Keep enough traffic on it to hold your access, too: after a model enters its Legacy period, existing customers can lose access after 15 days of inactivity. A Legacy model works until end-of-life, and after that Bedrock removes it from every Region, requests to it fail, and Bedrock doesn’t move your traffic automatically. Alarm when LegacyModelInvocations rises above zero.

Bedrock runtime metrics are dimensioned by ModelId, so you can see which model served a request but not which team sent it. Bedrock publishes these metrics both with and without the ModelId dimension, and a request that fails before Bedrock resolves the model appears only in the series without it, so filtering by ModelId undercounts errors. Bedrock offers three ways to attribute spend:.

According to recent reports, behind a gateway, Bedrock sees the gateway’s role, so have the gateway assume a role for each user with its own RoleSessionName or session tags. Cache those credentials for the session, because assuming a role on every request can exceed your AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) rate quotas. Requests keep succeeding when attribution breaks, so set an alarm for when Bedrock fails to deliver invocation logs.

Our usage records let us attribute usage by model, client, team and user, which we use only in aggregate for cost and capacity planning. We compute cost per task from the same four token counts, so we can compare token mix and cost between our evals and production.

According to recent reports, we can go from a model release to a deployment decision overnight. After one rollout, average weekly spend per user on model A was several times that on the previous model. We moved its heavy owners to a newer model. In their first full week, the group’s spend on its main model fell to about a seventh, with roughly the same number of requests. For every major model we use, our evals identify an equivalent we can rebalance to.

Sources indicate that after testing, stop the eval jobs and agent processes you started. If you enabled model invocation logging only for this walkthrough, disable it in each Region using DeleteModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration.

According to recent reports, after callers no longer use them, delete the application inference profiles you created using DeleteInferenceProfile. Remove IAM roles, policies, and resource tags created only for this walkthrough. Deactivate cost allocation tags used only for these tests. Delete test CloudWatch log groups and S3 log objects you no longer need.

We run four checks every time a model ships:.

It has been revealed that we chose Amazon Bedrock for access to multiple model families through one API. It lets us use our existing AWS access controls and logging while AWS manages the model infrastructure. We use evals to choose models for our work and observability to know when those choices need another look.

To go further, see these pages in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide:.

General Recommendations As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurity Additional Resources For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories Terms of Use The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use. Recommended Practices CISA recommends consumers take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Industry News: Neural Estimation of Irreversibility in Real and Simulated Limit Order Book Paths

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (260 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2610.16151v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A path indistinguishable from its own reverse carries no arrow of time, so time irreversibility is a necessary condition for a directed mechanism to be readable from trajectories alone. In finance it has been measured only on scalar series such as returns and volatility. We define the irreversibility rate of a coarse-grained limit order book path as the forward-to-reverse log-density ratio per event, and estimate it from three weeks of Nasdaq market-by-order data with an order-invariant MLP and a temporal convolutional network that receive identical blocks. For NVDA, the order-invariant and order-sensitive estimates are 0.036 and 0.054 nats per event, respectively. Their difference, the ordering increment, is 0.018. A surrogate preserving the coarse one-step transition table recovers 30 percent less irreversibility than the observed paths. The increment is positive for all twelve symbols on every held-out daytime date, and for NVDA in each session window. Across the twelve symbols, its share of the ordered rate increases roughly logarithmically with the spread in ticks. The increment changes more than tenfold with the coarse-graining scale. Neither a linear score nor any single feature group reproduces the full fitted rate. A queue-reactive simulator calibrated on the same days matches the market's ordered rate, 0.052 against 0.054, yet its ordering increment is 0.0006 against 0.018, building temporal asymmetry out of block composition instead of block order. We propose the ordering and scale profile of path irreversibility as a benchmark for order book simulators. Code and audit materials are available at https://github.com/hjyeo30/lob-irreversibility.

VeriMath: Human-in-the-Loop Generation and Verification of Curriculum-Aligned Mathematics Assessment Items

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (221 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.23456v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Automatic generation of mathematics assessment items is a growing area in educational artificial intelligence, yet classroom deployment remains challenging. Generated questions must satisfy multiple constraints: mathematical correctness, curriculum alignment, appropriate cognitive difficulty, and educator reviewability. While prior work has advanced text generation, reliable assessment authoring requires granular control over localized examination formats and expert educational judgment. To address this challenge, we present VeriMath, a generalized, human-in-the-loop framework for generating rigorous, curriculum-constrained mathematics assessment drafts. Using annotated reference items, the framework anchors generation to the requested examination section and cognitive reasoning level, then applies sequential automated verification and guided repair before submitting drafts for expert review. We evaluate VeriMath through a national curriculum case study using 4,555 mathematics items from the Vietnamese Grade 12 curriculum and 50 distinct generation requirements covering multiple-choice, true/false, and short-answer formats. Across two model backbones, the framework produces verifier-accepted drafts for 94% (47/50) of requirements per run. Blind expert evaluations confirm high mathematical accuracy and curriculum alignment, with strict teacher-readiness assessments accepting up to 56.8% of generated items. Analysis of rejected drafts reveals persistent domain-agnostic challenges involving formatting, statement validity, and solution-step completeness. These findings demonstrate that VeriMath can bridge generative AI and dependable educational applications by producing highly reviewable assessment drafts within tightly constrained national curriculum frameworks.

In a recent development, view CSAF Summary On October 21, 2026, the Node.js project released security updates addressing a critical vulnerability in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js, commonly referred to as "Node2Shell" (tracked as CVE-2026-111497). The vulnerability is an out-of-bounds write that could allow a remote attacker to cause memory corruption and potentially execute arbitrary code. This advisory covers the status of impact of various Siemens products. Siemens has released upcoming versions for several affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions. Siemens is preparing further fixes and recommends specific mitigations for products where fixes are not or not yet available. It has been revealed that I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory.

It has been revealed that orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk.

It has been revealed that I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me.

In a recent development, my first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi. That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim.

When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.

According to recent reports, strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090!

It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp, at 13.5 tok/s.

That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed.

Before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token?

llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU (--cpu-moe, --n-cpu-moe N, -ot "exps=CPU", or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache (--moe-cache-mib) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits.

Recent findings suggest that vLLM's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts, but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers, read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's big batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU.

Transformers offloads through Accelerate (device_map="auto", offload_folder), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before forward. For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them. No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory, so "offload to CPU" frees nothing.

I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM, and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags:.

Offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s.

If the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do it out of the box.

Strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the massive model on my laptop as the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work.

All of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming.

I started with OLMoE-1B-7B, which fits in memory, so I could compare every token with vanilla Transformers.

Industry observers note that first version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1 tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm, which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel.

The fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot pool: one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for vanilla.

Sources indicate that I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained, in huggingface/transformers#50717. To try it, install Transformers from that PR:.

Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next:.

That repo holds the output of the project's conversion script: the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table.

According to recent reports, experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout.

Industry observers note that the API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go through the per-layer quantization plan of #50245 rather than their own option.

Recent findings suggest that qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8. Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding table that needs its own disk path. So:.

The conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt peaks at 25.4 GiB. That's about the limit: I have to close the browser, or macOS starts swapping.

The model-specific bits (the n-gram table, Metal kernels) live in a small package, moe-expert-streaming, on top of the PR. The first version ran at about 10 tok/s.

Then I installed Strata on the same M5, with the same prompts:.

Strata 0.1.60 used IQ3_XXS experts. Both ran greedy, with thinking, MTP and speculative drafts off, and 1,024-token prefill chunks. The full setup and raw results are on the Space's details page.

Recent findings suggest that I also tried vllm-metal, vLLM on Apple GPUs through MLX, which recently got expert offloading. It streams the routed experts from an MLX checkpoint through a bounded cache, like this project. But it can't run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 32 GB, for the n-gram reason above: only the experts are streamed, and the n-gram tables stay in memory. That's 32 GB in the MLX checkpoints on the Hub, before the ~5 GB of dense layers and any expert cache.

According to recent reports, most of the time wasn't spent on experts. Here's what helped:.

Here's one MoE layer for one token, as it runs now:.

These are the final results after these optimizations on the same M5 with the same prompts:.

That's about 6% behind Strata on short decode, with slightly faster prefill, all through Transformers.

Most of what's left is host round trips, ~10 ms per token. Waking up after a sync is only ~1 ms of that. The rest is the GPU running dry while Python queues the next layer. Strata queues the whole token's work up front, and the GPU waits on a Metal shared event at each layer while the host reads experts. PyTorch doesn't expose that. I tried to fake it with a kernel spinning on a flag the CPU writes, and the GPU took anywhere from a second to never to see the write. The real fix would be a native op on PyTorch's MPS stream, with a risk of hangs, so I haven't built it.

Recent findings suggest that it runs at ~14 tok/s, close to Strata, and it's still too slow for how I use coding agents. Orthrus keeps doing the real work.

It has been revealed that transformers didn't beat Strata, and closing the last ~6% would take deeper changes in the stack, starting with control over that per-layer sync, which PyTorch doesn't give you today. The interesting part is how it got that close: streaming only the routed experts, a bounded cache that grouped_mm runs on as is, and a few targeted Metal kernels. There's no C++ extension in the project: just Python, Metal kernels compiled at runtime with torch.mps.compile_shader, and prebuilt kernels from the Hub. All the Metal kernels written for this experiment are now published on the Hub, and the project loads them from there.

Beating Strata was never the only goal, though. Building this was a great way to learn how MoEs and LLMs work from a systems perspective: how sparse the routing really is, how much an expert cache buys you, where memory bandwidth goes per token, and how much time the host and the GPU spend waiting on each other. Transformers makes all of that easy to poke at, one module at a time.

Sources indicate that the generic expert streaming implementation is in huggingface/transformers#50717, and the benchmarks are in the Space. Feedback on the approach and the API is welcome.

Thanks to Pedro, Lysandre and Arthur for their excellent feedback, and to Harry for helping test vLLM.

Finally, thanks to Niko Veit for Strata. Strata set the bar for what's possible with expert streaming on consumer hardware, and having those numbers to chase is what pushed this work as far as it went.

Shared Models, Selective Trading, and Order Flow

arXiv:2610.01897v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study whether the diversity of language models installed in a trading population carries over to the orders that reach the market. In simulated markets with five agents from each of three open-weight model families, we change only how a corporate announcement is presented and estimate each family's share of active orders. In two matched experiments, explanatory layoff text multiplies Mistral's participation by 5.3 (from 14.0% to 74.7% of opportunities) and raises its share of announcement-round orders from 17.5% to 57.4%. In a preregistered study of six upcoming events, adding one favorable and one unfavorable evaluation to identical facts changes active composition in a main sample and in an independently worded replication (average e-values of 6.3x10^25 and 6.7x10^40, against a threshold of 20). Within an event, the change reallocates on average 21% of active decisions across families in the main sample and 14% in the replication. The same reallocation appears under both wordings in three of the six events; in the other three, the families that gain differ. Evaluative text also lowers every family's average participation and lowers executed net flow in all twelve event-sample cells, and family contributions mostly reinforce one another. In the financing event of the first study, active composition changed substantially while net flow barely moved, because family responses offset one another. In a stylized market-clearing benchmark, price accuracy depends on both the number and the composition of active traders. The experiments do not identify why the models respond to evaluations, and they do not estimate effects on price accuracy.

Breaking: Introducing the Amazon SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, amazon SageMaker JumpStart gives you hundreds of open-weight foundation models you can deploy quickly.
  • Today we are launching the Amazon SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard, a new way to compare JumpStart models side by side on quality, speed, and cost, directly in Amazon SageMaker Studio.
  • The leaderboard is a new view of the JumpStart base models page in SageMaker Studio, right next to the Categories and All models views.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, amazon SageMaker JumpStart gives you hundreds of open-weight foundation models you can deploy quickly. That choice is powerful, but it also creates a real question: Which model should you start with? Comparing models usually means reading model cards one at a time and hunting for benchmark scores that different sources published under different conditions. Then you still must guess how each model will perform, and what it will cost, for your use case.

Today we are launching the Amazon SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard, a new way to compare JumpStart models side by side on quality, speed, and cost, directly in Amazon SageMaker Studio. In this post, we explain what the leaderboard demonstrates, define the key terms in plain language, and walk through how to go from a shortlist to a deployed model.

The leaderboard is a new view of the JumpStart base models page in SageMaker Studio, right next to the Categories and All models views. It uses the same search bar and filters you already know, and it opens on a leaderboard of large language models (LLMs). You see rankings immediately without answering setup questions first. For each model, it reveals two kinds of information:.

Because both kinds of numbers come from the same place and the same method, you can make a like-for-like comparison instead of stitching together data from different websites. At launch, the leaderboard covers 70+ models from providers including Meta, Google, Qwen, IBM, and Arcee, with more added over time.

The following screenshot reveals the leaderboard in SageMaker Studio, with benchmark scores, performance metrics, and estimated cost for each model.

Figure 1: Leaderboard overview in SageMaker Studio.

This section defines the terms the leaderboard uses: the quality benchmarks, the use case profiles and optimization goals that shape the performance numbers, and the performance metrics themselves.

A benchmark is a standardized test: a fixed set of questions with known answers. Running every model through the same test gives you a score you can compare. At launch, the leaderboard reports three reasoning benchmarks for LLMs:.

In a recent development, higher is better for all three. The leaderboard shows each benchmark separately rather than blending them into one number. That keeps the results transparent: You can weigh the benchmarks that matter for your application and check each score against the public definition of the benchmark.

Sources indicate that speed and cost depend on your workload and on how the model is deployed. Two menus above the leaderboard control which performance and cost numbers you see:.

Each optimization goal picks a different configuration:.

A note on cost: Estimated cost reflects SageMaker instance cost only, based on the on-demand hourly rate for the configuration’s default instance type. It does not include data transfer, storage, inference component costs, or discounts such as Reserved Instances or AWS Savings Intends. Your actual bill will vary. Use the AWS Pricing Calculator for billing estimates.

Recent findings suggest that published benchmark scores often come from different teams using different prompts, settings, and hardware, which makes them hard to compare. We took a different approach:.

For full details, including prompts, generation settings, and how configurations are measured, see JumpStart model leaderboard benchmarks.

Industry observers note that the following steps show how to go from browsing to a deployed model. You need access to SageMaker Studio and permission to deploy JumpStart models.

In SageMaker Studio, open the Models page, then select the Leaderboard view. The leaderboard keeps the same search bar and filters as the other views, and it has its own URL. You can bookmark it or share a direct link with your team.

The following screenshot shows the Models page with the Leaderboard view selected.

Figure 2: JumpStart base models page with the Leaderboard view selected.

Industry observers note that use the same search and filters you already use elsewhere in JumpStart to keep only the models that fit your requirements. Common filters include license, provider, and input and output modality. Start with hard requirements, for example a license that allows commercial use, before you look at scores.

The following screenshot indicates the leaderboard filtered by input modality, output modality, and license.

Figure 3: Leaderboard with filters applied.

Above the leaderboard, select the profile closest to your workload from the View benchmarks for your use case menu (default: Max Context). Then choose a goal from the Optimized for menu (default: Balanced). For a chatbot your customers interact with, Latency optimized is a sensible start. For overnight document processing, Throughput optimized or Cost optimized may fit better. The performance and cost columns update, and quality scores stay the same.

The following screenshots show the View benchmarks for your use case and Optimized for menus above the leaderboard.

Figure 4: View benchmarks for your use case menu.

Industry observers note that each column has a blue heatmap, so the top-performing models stand out at a glance: the deeper the blue, the stronger the result in that column. Sort any benchmark column to rank models by the metric you care about most. Use the column settings (gear icon) to hide metrics you don’t need, and scroll horizontally to see more. The model name columns stay frozen as you scroll, and a fade at the edge indicates when more columns are available.

The following screenshot demonstrates the heatmap and the column settings menu.

Figure 6: Heatmap and column settings.

Choose a model to open it. From there, you have options to deploy the model or, for models that support serverless customization, to customize it. If you deploy, choose the same use case and optimization goal you compared on the leaderboard. Each metric applies to the configuration it was measured on, and a different configuration can change quality, latency, throughput, and cost.

The following screenshot shows a model page with the Deploy and Customize options.

Figure 7: Model page with the Deploy and Customize options.

Suppose you are building an internal help-desk assistant. Employees ask questions and expect fast, accurate answers that follow a set response format. You need a commercially licensed model and want to keep costs predictable.

After filtering by license and choosing a chat-like use case profile with Latency optimized, your shortlist might look like this:.

Reading the table, Model A has the highest knowledge score but also the highest cost and the slowest first response. Model B scores almost as well, holds up on multi-step reasoning, and runs on a smaller, cheaper instance. For a help desk, where reasoning through a question and responding quickly matter more than the last few points of general knowledge, Model B is the better starting point. A bigger model is not always the better choice, and the leaderboard makes that trade-off visible in seconds.

From there, you would deploy Model B, test it with real questions from your help desk, and keep Model C in mind as a lower-cost option if quality holds up.

We’re continuing to expand the leaderboard. Areas we’re exploring include:.

It has been revealed that the SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard brings quality, speed, and cost together in one place, measured consistently on SageMaker. Instead of comparing numbers from different sources, you can filter to the models that fit your requirements, compare them on the configuration you proposal to run, and deploy with a few clicks.

To get started, open the Models page in SageMaker Studio and select the Leaderboard view. To learn more, see the following resources:.

Open the leaderboard, shortlist two or three models for your workload, and deploy them to test with your own prompts before you choose one for production.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (180 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

arXiv:2611.23454v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: Access to large-scale clinical text collections is crucial for advancing medical information retrieval research, including clinical note search, patient cohort identification, and domain-adapted retrieval models. However, real clinical notes are rarely available due to privacy regulations, which particularly limits progress for low-resource languages such as European Portuguese. We present LusoClin, a publicly released dataset of synthetic clinical notes in European Portuguese, created to support privacy-preserving research on clinical text retrieval. LusoClin was generated by pre-processing real clinical data, fine-tuning the open-source Llama 3.2 (3B) instruction-tuned model using Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation, and applying prompt-based clinical note generation. To facilitate semantic indexing and clinical search, the notes are automatically annotated with clinical entities using a BERT-based model. We evaluate LusoClin in terms of utility, fidelity, diversity, and privacy using automatic metrics and human evaluation. Results indicate that the dataset captures clinically relevant language patterns and can support downstream IR applications such as clinical document retrieval and domain-specific model adaptation, although annotators can often distinguish synthetic from real notes and some medical inconsistencies persist.

General Recommendations As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurity Additional Resources For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories Terms of Use The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use. Recommended Practices CISA recommends owners take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. Industry News: Intrinsic Geometry of the Stock Market from Graph Ricci Flow

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (208 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2510.15942v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We use the discrete Ollivier-Ricci curvature with Ricci flow to examine the intrinsic geometry of financial markets through the empirical correlation graph of the NASDAQ-100 index. A key feature of our approach is that we begin from an entirely ORC-spherical initial graph --- one in which all Ollivier-Ricci curvatures are strictly positive --- in direct analogy with Hamilton's (1982) foundational setting of manifolds of positive Ricci curvature. What happens to such a graph under discrete Ricci flow is an open question: no prior algorithm was designed for or tested on graphs where all curvatures are initially positive and community structure is entirely latent. We introduce ARCUS (Adaptive Ricci Curvature Unsupervised Surgery), which answers this question empirically: the Ricci flow of an ORC-spherical correlation graph develops a discrete neckpinch singularity, the curvature distribution polarising into two sharply separated populations with a self-selecting gap ratio $G \gg 1$. The procedure is genuinely recursive: each subgraph produced by surgery undergoes its own Ricci flow, following the Thurston geometrisation programme. The method is validated against the ten-stock benchmark of Mantegna (1999) and applied to the full NASDAQ-100 correlation graph, producing an eight-cluster hierarchical decomposition consistent with known market structure.

Industry News: Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A New Frontier and Use Cases

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2070 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads.
  • Every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory.
  • In a recent development, the challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs.

Every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next.

In a recent development, the challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome.

IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action.

In a recent development, foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to new series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic.

In a recent development, figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them.

Now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed, with nothing to deploy (documentation). On premises, the models can run within your own infrastructure using Confluent Platform for Apache Flink.(documentation). The models run on CPUs, without requiring GPUs.

Recent findings suggest that the models can support a range of mission-critical use cases, from helping keep production lines in spec and detecting unusual store activity to improving product-level planning. They can also provide signals to assess card payments and forecast trading volume to help place large orders. These building blocks can be applied across manufacturing, retail, banking, and airlines, bringing insights closer to where decisions are made.

See how time series and real-time context come together to create value:.

Businesses operate continuously. Orders are updated, payments arrive, shipments are delayed, and inventory changes throughout the day. Yet the information behind these events often sits across systems that update at different times or rely on periodic batch processes. When applications and AI agents act on outdated or inconsistent information, they risk making decisions that no longer reflect what is happening.

A Streamhouse addresses this by continuously capturing, processing, governing, and serving current business context. Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform brings together five capabilities—connect, stream, process, govern, and query—to make that context available to applications, analytics, and agents. Apache Flink transforms and enriches data as it flows, while Lightning Tables provide low-latency access to the current state.

Figure 2. The Streamhouse on Confluent: from existing data sources to current business context that agents, applications, analytics and lakehouses use anywhere.

Sources indicate that time-series models add predictive power to this architecture. Flink can prepare the data, invoke forecasting and anomaly detection, and make the results available alongside the events that produced them. Other models—including large language models, statistical models, and specialized machine learning systems—can contribute where appropriate.

Industry observers note that figure 3. The intelligence layer of the Streamhouse: time series models, large language models, and ML and statistical models, with orchestration across them.

This approach can help teams in four ways:.

-Scale model development. A pretrained model can provide a common starting point across many time series, reducing the need to develop and maintain a separate model for each one.

Sources indicate that -Refresh predictions as data changes. Forecasts can incorporate recent observations as part of a streaming workflow, subject to the model’s requirements and the pipeline’s configuration.

-Put signals closer to decisions. Forecasts and anomalies can be routed to operational applications sooner, where teams can combine them with business context, rules, and human judgment.

It has been revealed that -Run compact models on CPUs. The models are small enough to run on standard CPUs alongside the streaming pipeline, in the cloud or on premises, which can reduce the need for dedicated GPU infrastructure and simplify deployment.

Figure 4. Stream native time-series intelligence on Confluent.

The following scenarios illustrate how organizations could combine time-series models, streaming data, and application logic.

An ice cream line’s quality depends on overrun—the amount of air whipped into the mix. Today, the process engineer and operator rely on QA lab measurements taken after the tubs are filled. If a new cream lot or a warm, humid day changes the process, hours of production may already need rework by the time the team sees the result.

According to recent reports, to get ahead of the problem, a pretrained TTM model reads SCADA telemetry and QA measurements every 10 minutes. It forecasts the share of tubs expected to be in spec four hours ahead, along with a likely range.

Industry observers note that when the forecast falls below the plant’s target, an optimization process evaluates combinations of freezer draw temperature and airflow. Because the model takes these control variables as inputs, it can score each option before anything changes on the line. The operator approves the recommended setpoints, while routine adjustments can be automated within predefined guardrails.

Industry observers note that the outcome is a more proactive process: less rework, lower energy use per tonne, and more consistent quality. The same approach can be applied to ovens, dryers, kilns, and mills.

Figure 5. A forecast of product quality helps the operator evaluate freezer setpoints before making an adjustment.

Sources indicate that A store operations team monitors sales for thousands of products across hundreds of stores. Fixed thresholds often flag predictable weekend peaks while missing quieter changes, such as a product selling less than expected. As alerts accumulate, it becomes harder for the team to know where to focus.

Industry observers note that AI_DETECT_ANOMALIES gives each sales series an expected range based on its recent history. Each new reading is compared with that range at a confidence level the team chooses, without training a separate model for every product and store.

When sales fall outside the expected range, the signal can be combined with inventory and store data to help identify a likely cause and recommend a next step—for example, checking the shelf or replenishing stock. The same approach can be applied to machine sensors, API telemetry, meter readings, and payment volumes.

Figure 6. Store sales are compared with an expected range. In the view shown, recurring peaks remain within the range and no anomaly is flagged.

According to recent reports, A category planner and a replenishment team need to keep products available across every store without carrying excess inventory. But forecasts may be refreshed only once a week, often focusing on top-selling products, while the long tail is managed with simpler rules. When sales patterns change between planning cycles, one store can run out while another has too much stock.

Sources indicate that with AI_FORECAST, a pretrained model can forecast demand across products and stores. In this example, it produces a 28-day forecast with a P10–P90 range, refreshed as fresh sales data arrives. The planning application combines the forecast with inventory, lead time, and the planner’s chosen service level to calculate a reorder point.

It has been revealed that when stock is projected to fall below that point, an agent can draft a purchase order for review. The same approach can support planning for spare parts, staffing, ATM cash, and energy demand.

Figure 7. A store-level demand forecast informs a reorder point and a proposed purchase order for oat milk.

Fraud teams already rely on sophisticated rules and models to evaluate transactions. One continuing challenge is that a threshold applied across many cardholders may not reflect how each person normally spends.

A time-series signal can add that individual context. In this example, each payment is compared with an expected spending range based on the card’s recent history. A transaction outside that range is passed to the bank’s existing fraud systems as an additional input, alongside other signals and business rules.

The bank can then decide whether to approve the payment, request additional authentication, or investigate further. The decision and the signals behind it can be retained for review.

Figure 8.A payment outside the card’s expected spending range prompts a step-up authentication in an illustrative fraud workflow.

Recent findings suggest that an execution desk needs to divide a large order into smaller trades while managing its effect on the market. Historical volume curves offer a starting point, but today’s trading activity may look very different from the average.

On each one-minute bar, PatchTST-FM forecasts trading volume for the next 30 minutes, with a P10–P90 range. The execution algorithm uses that forecast to pace the order within the participation limit set by the desk.

Industry observers note that if a news event changes market activity, the algorithm can pause and replan. If trading is quieter than expected, it can reduce the size of each slice and signal that the order may take longer to complete. Each forecast and the resulting execution decisions can be retained in the audit trail.

Figure 9. Volume forecast informs the proposed execution schedule for a 100,000-share order.

A reliability engineer investigating an unusual sensor pattern may want to know whether similar behavior appeared elsewhere in the plant.

TSPulse can produce representations of time-series windows that support similarity search. In a separately built application, those representations could be indexed and used to retrieve historical patterns across equipment. An engineer could search for shapes such as a spike and recovery, a gradual rise, or a step change, then inspect the associated maintenance records and operating conditions.

Sources indicate that this application requires an embedding pipeline, an index, and access to the relevant context. Similarity can help narrow an investigation; it does not establish a root cause by itself.

Figure 10. Time-series embeddings can support a search for similar patterns across equipment and other signals.

The same models and building blocks can support different workflows across industries:.

Figure 11. The plant twin, from sensor to setpoint. A upcoming cream lot pulls overrun off target. The forecast reads the line, the agent proposes a new draw temperature and air flow, the operator approves, and the tubs are back in spec. Simulated data.

In a recent development, figure 12. The store twin, a store and its supply chain. A promo is coming for oat milk. The forecast prices in the promo and sets the reorder point, the agent raises a purchase order, the planner approves, and the shelf is full on promo day. Simulated data.

Sources indicate that banking: payments and the trading desk. The fraud lead wants to stop card testing without blocking good customers, and the trader wants a large order done without moving the price. Every card and every symbol is scored against its own expected pattern, event by event. Fraud and security holds the odd swipe before authorization, anomaly detection spots the unusual flow, and trading paces each order with the forecast volume.

Airlines: hub operations, fleet and network. Operations control wants to see a disruption coming while there is still time to act. Engine, gate and network streams are forecast and checked in real time. Anomaly detection catches the engine reading that drifts, production optimization rebalances gates and crews, and supply chain planning puts the spare part where the aircraft will be.

In every industry, the Streamhouse does the same work: Flink runs the Granite models to forecast, detect and optimize, Streaming Agents act on the live context, and people approve the exceptions.

Explore the models on Confluent to see how time-series intelligence can support real-time decisions.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (227 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.23445v2 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Deep vision models operating in resource-constrained environments depend heavily on low-bit quantization, yet compressing weights below 4 bits frequently induces catastrophic accuracy collapse. While mixed-precision recovery strategies aim to rescue accuracy by selectively retaining high-precision parameters, the fundamental mechanics of where and why these models collapse remain poorly understood. In this study, we systematically analyze the anatomy of quantization collapse across standard Vision CNNs (including ResNet and EfficientNet backbones) evaluated on the full 50,000-image ImageNet-1k validation set. First, we map the exact progression of degradation, demonstrating that collapse is highly non-linear and concentrated in late-stage pointwise projections and depthwise layers. Second, we introduce a structured, multi-step recovery waterfall that evaluates selective integer precision (INT4/INT8) and selective floating-point scales. We show that keeping less than 5% of critical layer activations in 8-bit precision recovers up to 92% of the accuracy lost during aggressive sub-4-bit compression. Finally, we bridge the hardware reality gap by evaluating deployment performance on standard ARM and x86 CPU architectures. We show that while low-bit quantization reduces memory storage requirements, standard runtime software bit-unpacking introduces a 1.48x to 21.5x execution slowdown depending on batch size, highlighting a critical trade-off between model footprint and actual edge throughput. Our findings provide a practical blueprint for navigating the limits of sub-4-bit deployment without sacrificing hardware performance.

Joint calibration of the volatility surface and variance term structure

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (254 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2509.08096v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: I study the calibration of option pricing models with an objective that combines errors on the implied volatility surface and on the variance term structure (VTS), and how the weight on the two trades one fit against the other. I then ask how the calibration affects hedges built from the fitted model. The setting is the stochastic volatility jump-diffusion model of Bates (1996), calibrated to S&P 500 index options on each trading day from 1996 to 2025. Calibrated to option prices alone, the model misses the VTS; however, a small weight on the VTS sharply reduces the error at the cost of a small loss in accuracy on the volatility surface and little change in hedging performance. I fit the model in two ways: unrestricted, with every parameter free, and restricted, with the spot variance pinned to an estimate from high-frequency returns and one jump-size law for all dates, estimated from option prices pooled across dates. This choice matters more for hedging than the weight does, and the closer fit to option prices does not necessarily have the lower hedging errors. The unrestricted fits match the surface more closely, but with rare and implausibly large jumps. Once options enter the quadratic hedge, whose positions depend on the whole fitted jump law, the restricted fits' hedging errors are as low or lower. The penalty on the VTS reduces the extreme jump sizes implied by the fitted parameters, but it does not explicitly exclude such jump laws.
