Tech Report: Amazon SageMaker Inference: 2026 launches in review, part 2

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3659 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that once a model is in production, the questions change.
  • For HyperPod Inference, it listed additional routing strategies, broader support for model serving frameworks, and expanded multi-Region networking.
  • To keep each section concrete, we follow one hypothetical team through the blog post.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that once a model is in production, the questions change. Teams want to know which configuration the model should run on now that traffic is real, how to fit more models onto GPUs they already pay for, what to do when the next model is too large for one machine, why requests wait in one Region while GPUs sit idle in another, and why latency rose when nobody changed anything. This post takes those questions in the order teams usually meet them.

For HyperPod Inference, it listed additional routing strategies, broader support for model serving frameworks, and expanded multi-Region networking. The Inference Gateway delivers the routing, and managed NVIDIA Dynamo is a latest serving framework. For managed endpoints, the roadmap pointed to deeper integration with the rest of the AWS AI landscape. Inference recommendations now run from Amazon SageMaker AI Studio, the SageMaker Python SDK, and the coding agents engineers already use, and endpoints can now route requests across Regions and accounts.

To keep each section concrete, we follow one hypothetical team through the blog post. In the spring, they launched a customer support assistant on a 70B-parameter model behind a single SageMaker AI endpoint, using the launches from part 1. By the fall, they need to support more product lines, adopt a larger reasoning model, serve customers in a second Region, and keep their GPU bill flat.

Figure 1: The five stages in this post and the introduces in each.

The team picked its first configuration from a benchmark run in April. Since then, they have added four LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) adapters, one for each product line, and the product team has set a target of 500 milliseconds for time to first token (TTFT) at peak load. The April configuration was never tested against either change. The engineers who will re-run the analysis work in notebooks and coding agents, and few of them use the console.

Inference recommendations launched in April as an API. Four updates since then make it available in more of the places teams work, and let it answer two harder questions: how many adapters an endpoint can carry, and how much concurrency it can take before it misses a latency target. A newly introduced agent skill brings the same expertise into coding agents.

Blog: Launching UI for generative AI inference recommendations in Amazon SageMaker AI.

The April launch automated instance, container, and optimization selection through APIs. Inference recommendations are now also available in SageMaker AI Studio as a guided, low-code workflow. In Studio, choose Jobs, then Inference optimization. Choose a use-case profile (Interact, Generate, Summarize, or Custom), an optimization goal (minimize latency, maximize throughput, or minimize cost), and a model from SageMaker JumpStart, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), the Model Registry, or an existing SageMaker model.

Sources indicate that sageMaker AI benchmarks candidate configurations on real GPU infrastructure using NVIDIA AIPerf and applies techniques that match the goal, such as speculative decoding for throughput or kernel tuning for latency. You compare the ranked results by TTFT, inter-token latency, throughput, and cost, and then deploy the chosen configuration to a real-time endpoint from Studio.

Blog: LLM optimization integration for Amazon SageMaker Python SDK.

Benchmarking and recommendations previously required SageMaker AI Studio or direct Boto3 calls. They are now part of the SageMaker Python SDK v3 (version 3.17.0 and later), the same interface teams use for training and deployment, so the workflow fits into notebooks, CI pipelines, and MLOps workflows. You can benchmark a live endpoint against your workload traffic, generate ranked recommendations for a latency, throughput, or cost goal, and deploy the top-ranked configuration to a real-time endpoint in a single call.

The SDK also supports longer workflows. You can run recommendation jobs in parallel to compare serving frameworks such as LMI and vLLM, and you can resume from a completed job so that deployment happens in a different notebook or pipeline stage without re-running the benchmarks.

Developer guide: Get recommendations for models with LoRA adapters.

It has been revealed that many teams use LoRA adapters to specialize one foundation model for several use cases. Each adapter kept in GPU memory reduces the number of concurrent requests the endpoint can serve, and the right balance depends on the instance type, the number of adapters, and the traffic profile.

Sources indicate that inference recommendations now accept adapters as Model Package Amazon Resource Names (ARNs), for adapters produced by SageMaker fine-tuning, or as S3 URIs, for adapters from external pipelines such as Hugging Face PEFT. SageMaker AI benchmarks combinations of adapter count and concurrency on real GPU infrastructure and returns ranked results for your workload. The output lists both formats for every adapter. The recommended deployment uses SageMaker Inference Components, with one component for the base model and one for each adapter, so you can add, upgrade, or remove an adapter without disrupting the base model or the other adapters.

Blog: Right-size generative AI endpoints with concurrency sweeps on Amazon SageMaker AI.

Right-sizing an endpoint means finding the highest concurrency it can sustain without breaching latency or error targets. Until now, that meant picking concurrency levels by hand, running a sweep, checking the results against the service level agreement (SLA), and repeating with a narrower range whenever the model or instance changed.

Recent findings suggest that inference recommendations now include a search that finds that boundary directly. Set search_recipe to max-concurrency-under-sla and supply targets for any combination of maximum TTFT, maximum time per output token, maximum end-to-end latency, and maximum error rate. The benchmarking engine (AIPerf) starts from a broad range, narrows it based on which probes pass or fail, and converges in fewer iterations than a linear sweep. The result reports the largest passing concurrency (feasible_max) or, if no level qualifies, the smallest failing one (infeasible_min).

According to recent reports, the search uses the same CreateAIWorkloadConfig and CreateAIBenchmarkJob APIs as concurrency sweeps. Optional parameters (concurrency_min, concurrency_max, search_max_iterations, and search_initial_points) bound the cost and speed up convergence.

Blog: Upcoming agent skill: Amazon SageMaker optimized generative AI inference for your coding agent.

According to recent reports, engineers increasingly ask their coding agent which instance and container to use. Without grounded knowledge and access to real benchmarks, the agent can only guess, and a wrong instance choice shows up later as missed latency targets or wasted spend.

The aws-ai-ml skill, available through the Agent Toolkit for AWS, gives coding agents such as Kiro built-in SageMaker AI inference expertise. Engineers describe what they need in plain language, and the agent can do the following:.

In a recent development, answers are grounded in measured performance and delivered as SageMaker Python SDK v3 code that engineers review and run under their own credentials. Setup takes about 10 minutes. The skill works with any agent that supports the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and in SageMaker AI Studio JupyterLab spaces.

It has been revealed that for the support team, one recommendation job that includes all four adapters, followed by a concurrency search against the 500 millisecond TTFT target, replaces the manual sweeps they ran in April. The engineer who owns it can start the job from a notebook or ask a coding agent to run it.

The support assistant does not run alone. An embedding model, a reranker, and a small classifier that routes tickets live in the same account, and each uses a fraction of a GPU. On a standard endpoint, each model copy still held a whole accelerator, so the team ran out of placement slots while GPU memory sat unused.

With Inference Components, you can host several models on one endpoint and size and scale each model separately. Until now, they were available only through the SDK and the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI). Every create, resize, and scaling policy had to be scripted, and there was no single view of what each model was using.

In the SageMaker AI console, you can now create, view, update, and delete inference components:.

The console calls the same SageMaker AI APIs as the SDK and CLI, so teams can start on the console and automate later, or manage scripted components visually.

Blog: SageMaker Inference now supports Multi-Instance GPU to maximize GPU utilization for model endpoints.

GPU partitioning uses NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) technology to divide one physical GPU into as many as seven partitions, depending on the accelerator. Each partition has dedicated GPU compute and memory, with complete hardware isolation. You define the partition layout when you create an endpoint for inference components and choose a partition type for each component. Applications keep invoking models by inference component name, so client code does not change.

According to recent reports, MIG isolates GPU compute and memory between partitions. Models on the same instance still share host CPU, host memory, networking, storage, and endpoint routing. You pay the standard rate for the full instance-hour, so the saving comes from placing more models on each instance, not from a lower hourly price.

Figure 2: Three small models on three GPUs, compared with the same models in partitions of one GPU.

For the support team, the embedding model, the reranker, and the classifier now run in separate partitions of one GPU on a single endpoint, and the team manages every component, including the assistant and its adapters, from the console.

Recent findings suggest that the team’s next model is a reasoning model whose weights alone exceed the GPU memory of any single instance. They have also noticed that long, retrieval-heavy prompts slow token generation for every other user on the endpoint. For a model this size, they move the workload to HyperPod Inference, which gives them dedicated clusters and Kubernetes-native control. The support assistant stays on managed endpoints.

Blog: Managed NVIDIA Dynamo on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference.

In a recent development, part 1 covered two building blocks for large models on HyperPod: disaggregated prefill and decode in Inference Operator v3.2, and KV-aware routing as part of the managed tiered KV cache. This launch adds multi-node serving and changes who operates the stack. NVIDIA Dynamo is an open source inference framework that provides multi-node sharded serving, disaggregated prefill and decode, and KV-aware routing. Teams could already run Dynamo on their own Kubernetes clusters, but they had to build and operate everything around it: placing all the nodes of a replica together, wiring Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) networking so prefill can hand its KV cache to decode at hardware speed, maintaining serving images, and recovering when one failed node takes down a multi-node replica.

With this launch, Dynamo runs as a managed serving engine on HyperPod. Dynamo makes the serving decisions: how the model is sharded, how prefill and decode are split, and where each request goes. HyperPod provides what those decisions depend on:.

The capabilities Dynamo brings to HyperPod are:.

In a recent development, there are three ways to start. Teams running Dynamo on self-managed Kubernetes can bring their existing DynamoGraphDeployment (DGD) manifests largely unchanged. Teams already on HyperPod Inference can patch the add-on and add a short dynamoSpec block to an existing InferenceEndpointConfig, which HyperPod converts into a DGD, while existing endpoints keep serving. Teams new to both can create a cluster with the add-on and Dynamo enabled from the console. In each case, clients call a standard OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so client code does not change.

Managed Dynamo supports vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM, and is available in the Regions where Amazon SageMaker HyperPod is available.

Figure 3: Managed NVIDIA Dynamo on HyperPod Inference.

Sources indicate that for the support team, the reasoning model runs as one sharded replica across several nodes, with separate prefill and decode pools. When a node fails, HyperPod replaces it and reschedules the replica without a page to the on-call engineer.

It has been revealed that the support assistant now serves customers in North America and Europe, so the team runs endpoints and HyperPod clusters in two Regions. During the US morning peak, requests queue in the US Region while GPUs the team already pays for sit idle in Europe. Some European traffic must also stay in Europe.

Recent findings suggest that routing decides whether capacity a team owns does useful work. It happens at four levels, and the debuts below cover one level each: which instance serves a request inside an endpoint, which pod inside a HyperPod cluster, which cluster across a fleet, and which Regional endpoint across Regions and accounts.

Figure 4: Routing across Regions and inside each endpoint or cluster, on both deployment paths.

Blog: Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoints now support KV cache aware routing.

Sources indicate that applications with long prompts or multi-turn conversations repeat a large prefix across requests. A model server can reuse the matching KV cache, but only if the next request reaches the instance that holds it. Prefix-aware routing, covered in part 1, fingerprints the start of each prompt and sends matching prompts to the same instance. Because it works from request history, its view of each instance’s cache becomes less accurate as the model server adds and evicts entries.

According to recent reports, KV-cache-aware routing uses the cache state the model container reports. The container publishes cache creation and eviction events to a central cache index, and SageMaker AI routes each request to an eligible instance that holds the longest matching cached prefix. This raises cache reuse for long-context prompts, multi-turn conversations, and workloads that share dynamic prompt prefixes.

It works with single-model endpoints and endpoints that use inference components, including LoRA adapters. It supports InvokeEndpoint, InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream, and the OpenAI-compatible API for Completions and Chat Completions payloads. You turn it on in the endpoint configuration. The first release requires an AWS-verified model container that implements the cache-event, tokenization, metrics, and OpenAI-compatible interfaces. You can track KV cache hit rate in detailed inference observability.

Which one to use. Prefix-aware routing works with any container and needs no container changes. KV-cache-aware routing needs a verified container and tracks the actual cache, which helps most when prefixes vary or caches turn over promptly.

Blog: Introducing Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference Gateway.

Industry observers note that inside a HyperPod cluster, capacity and demand rarely line up. One pod can be partway through a long-context request with its KV cache nearly full, while the next pod sits idle or already holds the prompt prefix or LoRA adapter the next request needs. Without visibility into that GPU state, new requests queue behind busy pods, and teams add GPUs to protect latency instead of using the ones they have. Each model also had its own endpoint, so clients had to track one endpoint per model.

The Inference Gateway is a GPU-aware router that installs with the HyperPod Inference Operator add-on and gives each cluster one OpenAI-compatible endpoint for all of its models. For each request, it reads live signals from every model pod and picks the best one, with weights you can tune per workload:.

Compared with round-robin routing, it reduced P99 TTFT by up to 97% on mixed GPU generations and by up to 98% under bursty traffic. It is available in all Regions where SageMaker HyperPod is available.

Blog: Keep inference running through regional capacity shortfalls with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI.

On managed endpoints, the same idea takes the form of the Cross-Region Inference Routing, managed routing that sends real-time and asynchronous requests across Regional endpoints a team has already deployed, in the same account or in different accounts. You group endpoints that serve the same model under a routing target, and the application invokes the target instead of a specific Regional endpoint. The router does not add capacity, replicate models, or deploy endpoints, and the existing invocation path keeps working.

The router replaces the failover logic teams build themselves today:.

Figure 5: Cross-Region Inference Router request flow.

Industry observers note that two months after the move, the team adds retrieval to the support assistant, and the average prompt length roughly doubles. TTFT is now higher than it was at launch, but nothing has failed, so every alarm stays green. When the team finds a better configuration, they will need to roll it out on large GPU instances that are hard to get more of.

Blog: Amazon SageMaker AI now detects latency drift, idle GPUs, and missed optimizations on your inference endpoints.

Sources indicate that amazon SageMaker AI now continuously monitors your generative AI inference endpoints and tells you when a change could improve performance or lower cost. Monitoring is on by default for SageMaker AI inference endpoints, with no setup required, and you can opt out of endpoints. SageMaker AI looks only at operational signals: latency, GPU utilization, and the endpoint’s serving configuration. It does not read your requests or responses. When a finding clears its confidence threshold, a notification appears on the AWS Management Console, and the same message arrives by email for teams that work in notebooks and the CLI. The recommended action opens the SageMaker AI agentic experience in SageMaker AI Studio with the finding already filled in, so the analysis, the comparison, and the deployment change happen in one conversation. Nothing deploys until you apply it, and you can turn monitoring off at any time.

There are three types of findings:.

Recent findings suggest that A standard rolling update replaces an endpoint one batch at a time, and every batch runs on newly provisioned instances. On a large GPU fleet, that means finding new capacity at every step, and an update can fail partway through when the next batch of instances is not available. Each released instance must also finish cleanup before it can be used again, which slows the rollout.

It has been revealed that sageMaker AI now updates models in place. It provisions one small batch of additional instances at the start, shifts traffic to that batch, and then updates the instances it frees, reusing them to roll the change across the rest of the fleet. The update still rolls out in stages, but it needs new capacity only once. For a fleet of 20 instances with a batch size of 2, the update acquires 2 new instances instead of 20. Customers do not need to change anything. As with container caching in part 1, the improvement applies automatically to rolling model updates.

Figure 6: A rolling revision acquires new instances at every step. An in-place rolling update acquires one batch at the start and reuses the rest of the fleet.

For the support team, a Drift Watch finding quantifies the TTFT regression and opens a new recommendation job against recent traffic. They roll out the updated model with one batch of extra instances, instead of finding new GPU capacity for every instance in the fleet.

The numbering continues from the 13 rolls out in part 1.

Recent findings suggest that 14. Inference recommendations in SageMaker AI Studio (July 2026). A guided, low-code workflow for ranked, benchmarked configurations, with deployment from Studio.

Sources indicate that 15. Inference recommendations in the SageMaker Python SDK v3 (August 2026). Benchmark, recommend, and deploy from a notebook or pipeline, with parallel and resumable jobs.

It has been revealed that 16. LoRA adapter support in inference recommendations (September 2026). Benchmarks adapter count against concurrency and deploys adapters as inference components.

In a recent development, 17. SLA-based concurrency search (September 2026). Finds the highest concurrency that meets TTFT, latency, and error-rate targets.

18. Agent skill for optimized generative AI inference (October 2026). Instance selection, benchmarking, and run comparison from MCP-compatible coding agents.

According to recent reports, 19. Inference Components in the SageMaker AI console (October 2026). Create, scale, and monitor each model on a multi-model endpoint without scripts.

20. GPU partitioning with NVIDIA MIG (October 2026). Up to seven isolated partitions per GPU, assigned per inference component.

21. Managed NVIDIA Dynamo on HyperPod Inference (November 2026). Multi-node and disaggregated serving, with HyperPod operating the platform underneath.

Industry observers note that 22. KV-cache-aware routing (November 2026). Routes each request to the instance that holds the longest cached prefix, based on cache events from the container.

In a recent development, 23. Inference Gateway for HyperPod (September 2026). One endpoint per cluster with GPU-aware routing, and up to 97% lower P99 TTFT than round-robin.

24. Cross-Region Inference Router. Routes across Regional and cross-account endpoints over PrivateLink, with overflow and residency guardrails.

Sources indicate that 25. Continuous performance monitoring. Detects latency drift, configuration gaps, and idle capacity, with a guided fix in SageMaker AI Studio.

Sources indicate that 26. In-place rolling model updates (November 2026). Rolls out model updates with one batch of additional instances at the start, then reuses existing instances across the fleet.

Recent findings suggest that by the end of the year, the support team serves four product lines from one base model, runs its small models on shared GPUs, serves a reasoning model that no single instance can hold, and routes traffic across two Regions with residency controls. It did not need to build its own benchmarking harness, failover logic, or drift monitoring to get there.

According to recent reports, part 1 argued that advantage in AI inference comes from operating an efficient inference stack. These 13 launches apply that argument to the months after launch day. The AWS Experience-Based Acceleration program can help your team put them to work by benchmarking your workloads and configuring your inference stack against your SLAs and cost targets.

On managed endpoints, we plan to extend in-place rolling updates in early 2027 with scale-in-first updates, which remove the need for any additional instances during a model revision.

It has been revealed that documentation and getting-started guides for every capability in this post are in the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide. Start with the section that matches your current problem. If your traffic has changed since you deployed, re-run inference recommendations. If you are short on placement slots, move small models onto partitioned GPUs. If requests queue while capacity you own sits idle, register your clusters and endpoints for cross-Region routing.

Training Language Models for Introspective Oversight

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (218 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.23365v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Language models increasingly exhibit behaviors that are difficult to detect in transcripts, such as reward hacking, deception, and sycophancy. Asking the assistant follow-up questions about its actions is unreliable, since models are generally not trained to report their own misbehavior. As a result, approaches to oversight typically involve querying external models. These face limitations: external transcript monitoring operates only on visible model outputs, and activation decoders lack full context and are prone to confabulation. We introduce introspective oversight, which trains a new role in the model to answer arbitrary questions about the assistant, rewarding answers that are verified against the assistant's actual behavior. We implement this by adding a separate, third-person observer role that answers these queries, which we can train solely for accuracy and separately from the assistant. On five held-out oversight evaluations, an observer trained on Qwen3.6-27B obtains a mean AUROC of 0.907, outperforming honesty training (0.864), transcript monitoring (0.828), and activation oracles (0.796). We further find that training an observer makes the assistant itself easier to monitor, with every baseline method improving on average when applied to the fine-tuned assistant. These results suggest that training models to answer verifiable questions about themselves is a tractable approach to overseeing unintended behavior.

arXiv:2508.05022v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose a framework for dependent default times where each name defaults when an increasing driver crosses an independent unit exponential threshold. As in Gueye and Jeanblanc (2022), the drivers may jump, so defaults may occur at stopping times of the reference filtration, including predictable ones, and a common jump may cause no, one or several simultaneous defaults. For general drivers, we derive the conditional joint survival law by a backward recursion; it is an explicit product of survival functions if and only if, for every set of names, the predictable reduction of the compensator of their first default time is deterministic. If, moreover, defaults avoid predictable stopping times, the law is a fatal shock law with hazards identified from the drivers; predictable default atoms can rule this out. Examples include L\'evy subordinators and, with random reductions but explicit laws, Liu's model and shot-noise drivers with memory.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, view CSAF Summary Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to retrieve sensitive system information, access application data without authorization, recover stored credentials, or intercept and manipulate network communications. The following versions of Dorsett Controls InfoScan are affected: InfoScan <=1.45.0 (CVE-2026-117659, CVE-2026-120157, CVE-2026-120255, CVE-2026-120260, CVE-2026-120271, CVE-2026-120298) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 8.1 Dorsett Controls InfoScan 5 Vulnerabilities Improper Certificate Validation, Exposure of Sensitive System Information to an Unauthorized Control Sphere, Use of Hard-coded Cryptographic Key, Missing Authentication for Critical Function, Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Water and Wastewater Systems Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Organization Headquarters Location: United States Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2026-117659 The InfoScan Electron desktop client improperly handles TLS certificate errors by accepting certificates without validating their trustworthiness. The client also configures Electron with nodeIntegration enabled, contextIsolation disabled, and webSecurity disabled. These settings weaken the client’s security boundaries. An attacker who is able to intercept or manipulate network communications may be able to present an untrusted certificate without the application rejecting the connection. Read More 1 Affected Product Dorsett Controls InfoScan <=1.45.0 Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fixDorsett Controls recommends updating affected versions of InfoScan to v1.46 or higher. To install the security patch, user administrators will need to log in to InfoScan and select System Maintenance from the menu. Once the System Maintenance application is open, select Check for Updates, and click the Install Now button in the Ready To Install section. If you are an offline customer (InfoScan has no internet access), you will need to download the upgrade from the Dorsett Controls Customer Portal by selecting the InfoScan Update tile, downloading the update, and following the instructions listed on the portal. The application uses these values to encrypt the MongoDB password before storing it in the Windows registry. Because the cryptographic material is embedded in the distributed application, an individual with access to the encrypted registry value and the application code may be able to recover the database password. These requests can trigger unhandled server exceptions that return detailed Node.js stack traces to the requester. The responses disclose internal filesystem paths, application directory names, source file locations, and line numbers. Recommended Practices CISA recommends consumers take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks: Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages. Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams. Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks. No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time. If you are an offline customer (InfoScan has no internet access), you will need to download the patch from the Dorsett Controls Customer Portal by selecting the InfoScan Update tile, downloading the update, and following the instructions listed on the portal.

Human-AI Mutualism Is Unstable under Capability Asymmetry

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (197 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.23322v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: One hope for a good human future alongside advanced AI rests on enduring mutualism: humans and AI will need each other, so the relationship will stay good for both. We argue that this hope fails as AI capability grows. Bargaining guarantees each side only what it would get if bargaining failed. For humans, this can be less than they had before AI. In a simple game-theoretic model, humans stay as well off as before AI without alignment only while they have leverage over the AI: either the AI depends on what they supply, or they can impose costs on the AI that are large relative to what the AI can produce. Once humans have neither kind of leverage, they stay as well off as before AI only if the AI is aligned with them. If the AI's goals are insatiable, the alignment required approaches perfect alignment as AI capability grows. Thus, mutualism is not a substitute for alignment. And when AI variants that keep more resources spread faster, alignment lasts only while misaligned variants are reliably sanctioned. In these two senses, human-AI mutualism is unstable.

#4512. Breaking: Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3729 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3729 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.
  • In a recent development, models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing.
  • Take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.

In a recent development, models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination.

Take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time.

According to recent reports, our earlier work (multi-harness RL, harness adapters) revealed that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations.

We leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2, OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6. The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol:.

Most RL frameworks train a re-implementation of the agent loop: the agent is written against the framework's own interface, such as verl's AgentLoop, SkyRL-Gym environments, rLLM's agent and environment classes, slime's custom rollout functions, or ART's client inside your own Python agent. Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. Recent work moves in the same direction: Agent Lightning v1.0 keeps the deploy-time harness in the loop through a proxy ("harnessed agentic RL"), and SkyRL's Harbor integration trains on Harbor trials, converting their chat histories into tokens for the trainer.

For this recipe we created a custom dataset for agentic coding with the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv. We combined together task retrieval of existing RL envs, task generation with Repo2RLEnv, task validation with OpenEnv, and sampling into a single data pipeline. This gave us the highest quality set of validated and relevant tasks to improve Qwen3.8-27B on agentic coding. In this section, we’ll walk through how we built it, so you can try it out on your own domains.

Sources indicate that RL training needs tasks the agent can attempt, a verifier that scores each attempt, and evidence that the verifier is right. A verifier that accepts wrong answers teaches the wrong behavior. A task that is already feasible will not teach the model anything.

According to recent reports, this section describes how we built the task set from three sources: two on the Hugging Face Hub and a third generated with Tasksmith, a pipeline in Repo2RLEnv. Every task passes an eligibility screen with openenv validate, and the same difficulty check against the base model, Qwen3.8-27B.

Each task uses the Harbor format, which Terminal-Bench 2.1 also uses. A broad search of the Hub for Harbor environments returned about 59,000 tasks, but they included duplicates, evaluation sets and tasks marked as not for training. We filtered down to just two Hub sources built for training and generated a third set ourselves:.

It has been revealed that we used Tasksmith to target gaps. We mapped the skills that our target benchmarks test (Terminal-Bench 2.1, the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, and DeepSWE), then chose pull requests that exercise them, such as HTTP streaming, filesystem operations and serialization. From 30 merged pull requests, Tasksmith produced 24 tasks in 10 Python repositories that passed its checks, 17 of them on a second run. Its checks do not replace ours, so these tasks go through the same pipeline as the rest.

In a recent development, A metadata screen runs first. It keeps tasks from training splits with permissive licenses. It drops duplicates, tasks marked as not for training, the 253 tasks in our target benchmarks, and any task from a repository those benchmarks use. We then ran the semantic checks from openenv validate on every task in fresh trials:.

Each trial ran as its own Hugging Face Job, which let us validate dozens of tasks at once. openenv validate offers the same option for any Harbor task:.

858 of 1,127 Hub candidates passed. Wrong-answer controls caught defects, including a Tasksmith task that accepted an incomplete implementation and a Terminal-Bench 2.1 verifier (regex-log) that accepted known-wrong answers. Most failures were infrastructure problems, such as images that did not start. Failed tasks stay in a rejected split with the failing check recorded.

Sources indicate that A valid task can still teach nothing. GRPO (group relative policy optimization) scores each attempt against the other attempts at the same task, so a task where every attempt passes, or every attempt fails, gives no learning signal. Before training, Qwen3.8-27B attempted each task 4 times, or 8 times for a stratified sample of six tasks per repository.

Of 442 scored tasks, Qwen3.8-27B solved 151 every time and 120 never. The 171 tasks it solved only sometimes form the qualified set. The figure below shows how the scores pile up at both ends and how they differ by source. The model solves most Go tasks every time, fails every attempt on more than a third of the SWE-smith Python tasks, and lands in the middle on 73% of the SWE-Gym tasks.

Qwen3.8-27B results on 442 scored tasks. Green marks the qualified tasks, which the model solves on some attempts but not all.

In a recent development, this example indicates how we filtered and validated 1,127 tasks to 278 which we included directly in the final dataset. The pipeline then took the remaining 522 rejected tasks, repaired and complexified them with Tasksmith and repeated validation.

The pipeline applies two filters: validation removes broken tasks, and the difficulty check keeps tasks the base model solves only sometimes. This section tests whether those filters change what the model learns. We trained four short runs of up to 50 steps, each on tasks from a different stage of the pipeline, and compared them with the base model on Terminal-Bench 2.1.

Each run trains Qwen3.8-27B with LoRA and GRPO, using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer, on 32 tasks. All four use the same agent harness (OpenCode with up to 48 model calls), the same settings and one 8×H200 Hugging Face Job, and the reward is the verifier's pass or fail. The task sets differ in how they were filtered:.

According to recent reports, the figure below demonstrates how the tasks impacted model learning. The table lists each run's steps and the checkpoint we evaluate. The chart tracks training reward across subsets of tasks with differing validation status.

harness-hub/agentic-coding-envs holds 871 tasks from 35 repositories. Hub tasks are capped at 40 per repository, so no single project dominates. The table below shows what each source contributes. The dataset has two views: every accepted task, and the qualified subset for GRPO training. Rejected attempts stay in a separate config.

We leveraged the stable version of AsyncGRPOTrainer from TRL, with the main advantage of the trainer being that it does not wait until all rollouts are completed before moving to the next training optimization step.

For more detailed reading on the trainer and its building blocks, please refer to the AsyncGRPO blogpost.

It has been revealed that to obtain our final harness adapters, we trained LoRA adapters on top of Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer. The adapters were attached to the model using the all-linear flag. To maximize the training efficiency, thinking mode was turned off during rollout stages, and we evaluated our final adapter with and without thinking for broader comparison.

The final reward function consists of the verifier's correctness, combined with a small tool-efficiency bonus (0.1, derived from early experiments from the previous iteration of harness adapters which showed that 0.1 worked best).

We performed a small LR sweep on 50 steps using Termgrade environments (1e-5, 5e-5 and 1e-4) and noticed that 1e-5 barely moved training correctness (from 0.52 to 0.50), 1e-4 collapsed the rollouts instead of improving them (turns per rollout moved from 18 to 6, with entropy rising), and only 5e-5 clearly improved (from 0.49 to 0.60 by step 40). Longer 5e-5 runs then revealed signs of instability (collapsing rollout lengths, rising entropy), so we settled on 2e-5 for the final runs.

In a recent development, each harness adapter was trained using NVIDIA 2xB200 GPUs, with one GPU allocated for the vLLM server and the other allocated for the training process. We first performed some stress testing to maximize the amount of RL tasks that can be trained within a single optimization step. For that, we ‘maxed out’ the --token-budget argument from AsyncGRPOTrainer to its limit for the setup that we had. The chart below reveals the evolution of the number of groups per step for each harness (in blue: Pi, green: OpenCode and orange: Hermes).

As the model gets better and better during training, it is able to fit more and more groups during each training step, which diversifies the signals that the model gets at each optimization step.

The final data mixture consists of 750 tasks from harness-adapters RL environments and 300 tasks from termgrade. In order to maximize the diversity of the sampled tasks during training, we have slightly customized the data sampling strategy, which will be explained below:.

It has been revealed that before training, the tasks are put in a fixed order that interleaves them by family (i.e., their repository for our generated RL environments. For Termgrade, we just sorted them by name since each task is considered as its own family), so every training step mixes as many repositories as possible while following the distribution of the mixture.

Recent findings suggest that we also plug the safeagents tool, in order to block any misbehavior from the model during training. The final plugin (which consists of the regex and pattern rules specific to the RL tasks and test path) is hosted in harness-hub/qwen-safeagents-plugin and can be used out of the box using the latest version of safeagents in case anyone wants to reproduce the training setup.

Industry observers note that the number of blocked tools from safeagents decreases consistently during training, which indicates that the model gets ‘safer and safer’ after each optimization step. Below is a diagram of the safeagents blocked calls per 1000 tool calls, by training step, for each harness adapter.

Industry observers note that merging models often combines their capabilities while keeping most of what each one could do. Once the three harness adapters were trained, we asked two questions. Does merging them cost accuracy? And can a single "super-adapter" be accurate and efficient under every harness?

We started by comparing the weight updates of the three adapters, layer by layer. The cosine similarity between any two of them is about 0.01–0.02: each adapter pushed the model in a nearly orthogonal direction during training. That's the best case for merging, since the updates barely interfere.

According to recent reports, we concatenate the three LoRA adapters along the rank dimension (PEFT's combination_type="cat"). The merged adapter has rank 96 (3 × 32) and applies exactly w · (ΔW_pi + ΔW_hermes + ΔW_opencode). Prior work on merging (task arithmetic, TIES, KnOTS) finds that scaling each update below 1 works best, so we compared three weights on all 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, under each harness, with the step-120 adapters:.

The plain sum over-applies the updates. The agents become very short (13 tool calls per task, against 49 for the base model), and while Hermes peaks at 62.8%, pi falls back to the base model's level. The average dilutes each harness's own update. ½ gives the best balance, so we built the final super-adapter from the released checkpoints (pi step 160, hermes step 160, opencode step 150) at weight ½.

Under each harness, on the tasks every run graded (50–51 on SWE-bench Pro, 82–85 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), one attempt per task (in parentheses, the efficiency gain with respect to the base model):.

"Thinking" is the chat template's thinking mode at its default effort (xhigh). The specialists were trained and served with thinking off.

With thinking off, the super-adapter improves on the base model on all six harness–benchmark pairs (mean pass@1 39.5% → 49.0%; 71 tasks newly solved vs 34 lost, p < 0.001).

Despite not being trained at all with thinking on, it's the strongest model we evaluated with thinking mode. Against the base model thinking at the same effort, it wins on five of six pairs and ties the sixth (mean 55.5% → 63.5%; 67 newly solved vs 37 lost, p = 0.004). The largest gains are on SWE-bench Pro: +16 points under hermes and +20 under opencode. Under pi on SWE-bench Pro, where thinking alone already reaches 74%, it ties.

It has been revealed that use the specialist harness adapters when thinking off. Each harness's own adapter is ahead on four of six pairs, by the most under pi (64.0% vs 46.0% on SWE-bench Pro, 56.5% vs 48.2% on Terminal-Bench). Splitting one model across three harnesses costs pi the most of its gain. If you only use one harness and keep thinking off, take its specialist.

The super adapter is also much more efficient. On the tasks both the base model and the super-adapter solve, with thinking off, it makes 53–73% fewer tool calls and generates 44–60% fewer tokens per task, with fewer tool calls on 111 of 130 tasks. With thinking on, it still cuts tool calls by 31–48% and tokens by 24–43% on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench, tool calls drop by 19–25% and token counts stay about the same.

The ½ weight was chosen on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the step-120 adapters, so the Terminal-Bench numbers are slightly optimistic; SWE-bench Pro played no part in the choice. Full paired results are in the super-adapter's model card.

This section reports what happened during training, then how the adapters score on held-out benchmarks inside and outside their own harnesses.

Training ran for a cumulative total of 598 steps, with a total of 78,114 samples trained, which consists exactly of 167M trained tokens.

During training, we see a clear signal that the model learns to solve tasks in fewer and fewer steps, with no clear sign of saturation. Despite having some clear increasing trend sometimes, training correctness seems to overall stay flat. This can be explained by the fact that the model meets new tasks during training, but the number of groups that fit in a step’s token budget more than doubles as trajectories get shorter. The accuracy gains show up on the held-out benchmarks in the section below.

On the other hand, safeagents was able to block multiple suspicious attempts. Across the three training runs, a total of 1.3M tool calls have been checked, and a total of 647 tool calls have been blocked.

This section covers the evaluation setup, the in-harness results, transfer across harnesses, and an out-of-distribution check.

We evaluate each adapter inside the harness it was trained in, on two agentic coding benchmarks: all 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 (1 hour and 100 agent steps per task) and the 51 hardest tasks of SWE-bench Pro (2 hours and 100 agent steps). We cap the maximum number of tokens per task to be 131072. We do not tune the agent settings and use the default setup for all harnesses. For example, Pi does not keep previous reasoning turns while OpenCode and Hermes do, which mainly affects the SWE-bench Pro results due to rapid context overflow. Therefore you cannot compare the results across different harnesses (using Pi does not necessarily lead to better results than Hermes or OpenCode), but it is fair to compare results within the same harness and draw conclusions.

Every rollout runs through the same Harbor and OpenEnv stack as training, in HF sandboxes, with one attempt per task at temperature 0.8 and thinking off. Each LoRA checkpoint is merged into the base weights and served alone with vLLM on a single GPU, at the same concurrency as the base model's eval.

For all the evaluation benchmarks, we report the pass@1 as well as the number of tool calls, total turns, for all tasks and for solved tasks.

For openness, all model trajectories for final evaluations are pushed in this public bucket: harness-hub/harness-adapters-trajectories.

All three specialist adapters beat the base model under their own harness, on both benchmarks. On SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), pi goes from 39.2% to 64.7% (+25.5 points: 15 tasks newly solved vs 2 lost, p = 0.002), hermes from 29.4% to 43.1%, and opencode from 35.3% to 51.0%. On the full Terminal-Bench 2.1, pi gains +16.3 points (16 vs 2, p = 0.001) and hermes +14.1 (19 vs 7, p = 0.03). Opencode gains +6.0 overall, and +13.6 on the 66 tasks that played no part in choosing its checkpoint (12 vs 3, p = 0.035).

According to recent reports, the adapters also solve tasks much more efficiently: on the tasks both they and the base model solve, they make 56–72% fewer tool calls per task on SWE-bench Pro and 53–70% fewer on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The single super-adapter beats the base model under all three harnesses too (+6 to +18 points on SWE-bench Pro, +5 to +10 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), with just as large a cut in tool calls (53–73%). It keeps less of each specialist's gain with thinking off, most under pi, but with thinking on it beats the base model thinking at the same effort on five of six harness–benchmark pairs (see the super-adapter section). Each model card has the full paired results.

To answer this question, we also evaluated the pi harness adapter under Hermes Agent and OpenCode.

Industry observers note that under OpenCode it matches OpenCode's own specialist on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (44.8% → 54.0%, against 46.4% → 52.4%). Under Hermes it keeps about two-thirds of the specialist's gain (46.3% → 56.1%, against 44.7% → 58.8%), with the same ~45% cut in tool calls in both. Therefore it seems that the newly learned capabilities are transferred across harnesses.

What happens if we evaluate in out-of-distribution tasks, outside the harnesses the adapters have been trained with?

In a recent development, we ran all five models on 300 AutomationBench tasks which consists of business-automation workflows evaluations, with AutomationBench's own agent loop instead of Pi, Hermes or OpenCode. This way, we can cross check two different questions: can the model solve problems outside SWE-related tasks? What happens when the model is being put outside the harness it has been trained with?

Results show that the adapters stay close to the base model. Pi and OpenCode are slightly ahead (27.0% and 25.3% pass@1 against 23.0%), the merged adapter is level (23.7%), and Hermes is a few points behind (17.7%). The differences are within noise, except perhaps Hermes, therefore RL inside the harnesses neither transfers clearly to this very different setting nor breaks the model on it.

It has been revealed that we appreciate the feedback from the customers and the community, initial testing and results from the community seemed overall extremely positive, and we wish to continue in this direction in the future. We also saw some surprising results, such as users reporting that the harness adapters work really well under Qwen3.8 derivatives, such as Swift-1.5.

This question is an open question we thought about, post-release. After inspecting carefully the generated trajectories from the evaluation benchmarks, it turns out the model, under non-thinking mode, tends to generate some short text before proposing a tool call, as opposed to the base model which generates the tool calls barely without any text beforehand.

According to recent reports, this phenomenon can be seen as a sort of ‘reasoning leakage’, where the model learns to ‘escape’ from its non-thinking version to its thinking version by generating some text that can sometimes look like reasoning traces (e.g.: ..wait? ..let me see, etc.). A recent paper also describes behavior from LLMs during the RL stage very well.

Does this invalidate our models? We do not think so, as the final results are still valid; under the exact same conditions (fixed token budget) our adapters do outperform the base non-thinking model (by far) and match the performance of the thinking version, while being much more token efficient. This has been further confirmed by the positive feedback from the community.

However this raises the need of a proper follow up work, where we will try to re-apply the same pipeline for pure thinking models, as well as exploring hybrid thinking / non-thinking training, to better understand the behavior of RL training on hybrid thinking models. We will share with the community our next findings (and harness adapters), once we get conclusive results.

Throughout this work, we demonstrated that RL training your model inside your target harness leads to more efficient and therefore more accurate final models, when evaluated under the same conditions. This observation is in line and in continuation with several previous work from Hugging Face teams, such as multi-harness-RL or the early iterations of harness adapters.

In the future, we will explore applying this recipe to more models, while better studying the training strategies for hybrid thinking / non-thinking models.

In a recent development, we also share to the community openly the full recipe and pipeline to reproduce everything, and invite everyone to build their own RL tasks, derived from their own codebase, or any relevant materials, and apply the same training recipe and ideas to their favorite model and harness for more efficient agentic models. We hope this blogpost will serve as a starting point for builders to build and share their own harness adapters in the future.

#4511. A joint framework for SPX, VIX and VXX

A joint framework for SPX, VIX and VXX

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (144 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.25047v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Options on VXX bring the dynamics of the VIX futures curve into the joint SPX-VIX calibration problem. We construct a common model by specifying the VIX and then recovering instantaneous SPX variance from the requirement that its risk-neutral conditional expected average over the next thirty days equals the squared VIX. With truncated signatures of time-extended polynomial diffusions, this recovery reduces to finite-dimensional linear algebra and gives explicit access to the futures underlying VXX. The same specification therefore governs equity variance and rolling volatility exposure. To accommodate flexible specifications while respecting variance nonnegativity, we develop a regularized model and quantify the pricing errors of its tractable VIX and VXX proxies. Applications to short-dated option smiles illustrate joint calibration across the three markets, with Monte Carlo estimates of the proxy error bounds well below quoted bid-ask spreads.

Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • CISA has added four latest vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.
  • CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.
  • These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CISA has added four latest vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2024-10441 Synology DiskStation Manager (DSM) Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output Vulnerability CVE-2026-40217 BerriAI LiteLLM Unprotected Alternate Channel Vulnerability CVE-2026-90436 Apache Axis Unsafe Reflection Vulnerability CVE-2026-90817 Vanderbilt University Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) Code Injection Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not right now listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

Industry observers note that while BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not presently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.
